summary: Amina Ali Qassim says her family escaped their home on Yemen's Birim island just before missiles destroyed it during the Saudi aerial bombardment, spending the night in a mosque with her terrified infant granddaughter. At first light, 25 people from four families crowded into a boat and made a five-hour crossing of the Bab al-Mandab Strait to Djibouti. The government is temporarily housing them in an unfinished orphanage in Obock before they move to tents outside town, while the United Nations expects thousands more refugees. Qassim has been unable to contact her two daughters trapped in Taiz and fears for them.

Australian police arrested five men aged 18 or 19 in Melbourne on Saturday in a counterterrorism operation, subsequently releasing three pending further inquiries. Sevdet Besim, 18, was charged with conspiring to commit a terrorist act and denied bail, while a 19-year-old remained in custody without having appeared in court. Federal Police acting deputy commissioner Neil Gaughan said evidence and other information suggested the alleged plot was inspired by ISIS. Authorities said the suspects intended to attack police at an Anzac Day ceremony on April 25, marking the centennial of the Gallipoli Campaign, and that the public was also at risk. Police said the suspects were associates of Nadun Haider, 18, who was killed while stabbing officers at a police station in September. Victoria Police acting deputy commissioner Shane Patton emphasized that the suspects acted as individuals and did not represent a religious, cultural or national group. Prime Minister Tony Abbott cited earlier extremist incidents, including December's Sydney cafe siege, in which two of the 17 hostages and the gunman died, and February charges against two men accused of planning terrorist activities in Sydney. Abbott said about 100 Australians were fighting with terrorists in the Middle East and another 150 people in Australia supported them through funding and recruitment. He had announced tougher citizenship laws in February, and authorities had suspended passports of people suspected of terrorist activity. Police said this particular threat was fully contained, and Abbott encouraged Australians to continue their normal lives and attend Anzac Day commemorations.

Hundreds of decomposed corpses were discovered buried in shallow graves in the streets of the northeastern Nigerian town of Damasak this past weekend, according to local officials and a resident, after the town had recently been freed from the Boko Haram terror group in a joint Nigerian-Chadian military operation. Damasak residents who participated in the exhumations put the figure at more than 400, and Abubakar Kyari, a senator-elect for the region, said the victims included men, women and children murdered by Boko Haram when they seized the area in November.

ISIS claimed responsibility for a suicide car bomb attack Friday near the U.S. Consulate in the Kurdish Iraqi city of Irbil, according to several Twitter accounts linked to the terror group. At least four people were killed and 18 injured, police said, while Peshmerga spokesman Hazhar Ismail said three civilians were killed and five others were injured. All U.S. Consulate personnel were safe and accounted for following the explosion, U.S. State Department spokeswoman Marie Harf said. Security personnel fired at the car, which exploded but did not reach the consulate, a police official said.

James Best, best known for his portrayal of bumbling sheriff Rosco P. Coltrane on TV's "The Dukes of Hazzard," died Monday after a brief illness. He was 88. Best died in hospice in Hickory, North Carolina, of complications from pneumonia, said Steve Latshaw, a longtime friend and Hollywood colleague. Although he'd been a busy actor for decades in theater and in Hollywood, Best didn't become famous until 1979, when "The Dukes of Hazzard's" cornpone charms began beaming into millions of American homes almost every Friday night. For seven seasons, Best's Rosco P. Coltrane chased the moonshine-running Duke boys back and forth across the back roads of fictitious Hazzard County, Georgia, although his "hot pursuit" usually ended with him crashing his patrol car. Among the most popular shows on TV in the early '80s, "The Dukes of Hazzard" ran until 1985 and spawned TV movies, an animated series and video games. Several of Best's "Hazzard" co-stars paid tribute to the late actor on social media. Born Jewel Guy on July 26, 1926, in Powderly, Kentucky, Best was orphaned at 3 and adopted by Armen and Essa Best, who renamed him James and raised him in rural Indiana. Best served in the Army during World War II before launching his acting career. In the 1950s and 1960s, he accumulated scores of credits, playing a range of colorful supporting characters in such TV shows as "The Twilight Zone," "Bonanza," "The Andy Griffith Show" and "Gunsmoke."

Feidin Santana's video of North Charleston officer Michael Slager firing eight times at the fleeing, unarmed Walter Scott led to Slager's dismissal and arrest on a murder charge. Santana told CNN another officer ordered him to stop recording, and said he saw neither Scott grab a Taser nor officers perform CPR, observations that differ from Slager's account and a police report, respectively.

The latest high-profile digital incursion, in December, attempted to steal data from South Korea's nuclear operator, including plant blueprints and personnel information. Codes used in the attack were said to be similar in pattern to those used by the North Koreans, South Korean authorities said.

Koch Industries' recent announcement that it will "ban the box" -- i.e., remove from its job applications the check-box that asks about convictions -- is a big step forward in the movement to break down barriers to employment for job-seekers with records. "Ban the box" doesn't prohibit background checks, it only postpones them until later in the hiring process. So far, 16 states and more than 100 cities and counties have adopted fair-chance hiring policies. Now it's time for President Obama to lead the way and embrace fair-chance hiring of people with records.

The migrant crisis that has suddenly drawn hundreds of journalists to Sicily has been brewing for years, but in the past 10 days, with as many as 1,600 deaths in the Mediterranean, suddenly minds are focused -- for now. The fall of Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi's regime, which we reporters covered so avidly, was followed by chaos, which we in the news media largely neglected, focused as we journalists were on the next catastrophe, the Syrian civil war. In that chaos, the business of human trafficking has boomed. Aware of the tragedy underway, however, Italians are alarmed at the prospect that this year alone as many as a million migrants could arrive in Europe, according to one European Union official. That is certainly the case in the Sicilian port of Catania, where many migrants arrive. The city's mayor, Enzo Bianco, insists city residents bear no ill will toward the migrants, but says Catania, and Sicily cannot absorb the ever-growing numbers. The rest of Europe must help carry the burden. Two northern regions, Veneto and Valle d'Aosta, have declared they will no longer accept new migrants. Others, however, insist Italy must keep its doors open.
